checkpoints: A producer never talks to a queue directly; it only calls publish(exchange, routingKey, payload), and the exchange's type decides where the message goes, not the producer.
A direct exchange matches the message's routing key exactly against a queue's binding key, delivering on a match and silently dropping on no match, making it strict one-to-one routing.
A fanout exchange discards the routing key entirely and broadcasts a copy to every queue bound to it, so it is the number of bound queues that decides the fan-out.
If two independent systems shared one queue on a fanout exchange, the broker would round-robin between them, turning pub/sub into a work-queue where each message lands on only one.
A topic exchange matches the routing key against a wildcard pattern where * stands for exactly one token and # stands for zero or more tokens.
A binding like logs.# catches logs.error, logs.info.db, or bare logs but never metrics.cpu, letting you route on several dimensions at the cost of a pricier pattern match.

The routing algorithm lives entirely in the exchange's declared type, so swapping direct for fanout for topic reshapes the whole delivery topology while the producer's publish() call never has to change.

Calling a slow or flaky task synchronously inside the request makes the user wait for it to finish, and if the handler times out or the process dies mid-flight that work is lost entirely — that is exactly the limit of the HTTP request lifecycle: it has a timeout and dies with its handler, with no notion of leaving work to run later.
A job queue fixes this gap by turning the task into a durable record and returning the response right away, decoupling accepting the request from executing it.
A separate worker process, apart from the API, pulls that job and processes it, and because it is its own process it scales independently of the API.
Because the job already lives on a durable store, an API restart doesn't lose it and the worker just picks it back up.
A job queue adds retries with backoff for when the downstream is flaky.
A job queue adds the ability to delay or schedule execution for a future point in time.
A job queue adds priority so important jobs get picked first.
A job queue adds a dead-letter queue to quarantine permanently-failing jobs instead of letting them block the whole queue.

BullMQ's jobId-based deduplication only works while a job record with that id still exists in Redis; once BullMQ forgets a job, re-adding the same id is treated as a brand-new job rather than a duplicate.
`removeOnComplete: true` deletes a completed job — and its id — from Redis the instant it finishes, immediately freeing that id up for reuse.

Pairing a deterministic jobId for idempotency with `removeOnComplete: true` creates a race: once the original job has completed and been wiped, any duplicate enqueue for the same logical work (a redelivered webhook, a client retry) no longer collides with anything and gets processed a second time.

This gap is easy to miss in review because the code still reads as idempotent, and tests that only call add() twice back-to-back before the first job finishes never exercise the complete-then-duplicate sequence that triggers it.

For a job with a real side effect, like sending an email, a duplicate that slips through silently double-fires that effect; on a payment or credit job the same gap becomes a double-charge, so this is a correctness blocker rather than a style nitpick.

The fix is to stop hard-deleting completed jobs immediately: bounding `removeOnComplete` with an age/count retention window wide enough to outlive realistic duplicate-arrival windows keeps completed jobs around long enough for a later duplicate add() to still collide with them.

Idempotency can also be decoupled from job history entirely by keeping a separate durable `processed:<jobId>` key with its own TTL in Redis and checking it before enqueueing, so the dedup guarantee no longer depends on how long BullMQ happens to retain completed jobs.

The memory-saving intent behind `removeOnComplete: true` is legitimate, but a bounded retention window addresses unbounded job history growth without reopening the dedup gap that instant deletion creates.

Verifying the fix requires a test that enqueues a jobId, lets the worker complete it, enqueues the same jobId again, and asserts the side effect fired exactly once — reproducing the specific complete-then-duplicate timing the bug depends on, not just two immediate back-to-back enqueues.

Calling `await channel.waitForConfirms()` immediately after every `channel.publish()` inside a loop forces each message to complete a full round-trip to the broker before the next one can even be sent.

`waitForConfirms()` resolves once all currently outstanding publishes have been acknowledged by the broker — it is designed to be called once after a batch of publishes, not after each individual one.

Placing the wait inside the loop turns what should be pipelined I/O into N sequential round-trips, so the wall-clock cost scales as roughly N × round-trip time instead of a single round-trip for the whole batch.
This cost is invisible when testing with a single message, since one round-trip is fast, but becomes dominant once the batch reaches hundreds or thousands of orders.
Publisher confirms are asynchronous by design — durability only requires that the producer eventually learns which messages the broker accepted, not that it pause after each send.
The fix is to publish the entire batch, or a bounded chunk of it to cap in-flight memory, back-to-back with no await between sends, then call `waitForConfirms()` exactly once after the loop.
Batching the wait lets the broker process the whole burst concurrently, collapsing many round-trips into one without sacrificing the durability guarantee publisher confirms provide.

The fix can be validated with a benchmark that measures wall-clock time publishing N=1000 messages both ways, expecting the batched version to stay roughly flat as N grows while the per-message version scales linearly with N.
A Redis key created by `hmset` on `rl:<clientId>` with no TTL/PEXPIRE ever set on it stays in Redis permanently, regardless of whether the client that owns it ever comes back.

Every distinct, never-before-seen `clientId` produces a brand new hash key, so the total key count in Redis grows with the number of unique identities ever observed over time, not with how many clients are concurrently active.

Churning or one-time client identifiers — rotating mobile session ids, one-off request ids, IPs behind NAT — are what turn this into a real production leak, since each one mints a key that is never reclaimed.

The leak stays invisible in a test suite that reuses only a handful of familiar client ids, because that workload keeps hitting the same small set of keys instead of minting new ones, so Redis memory never appears to grow.
The check-then-decrement token math itself is correct; the bug is purely the missing expiry, not a logic error in how tokens are read, refilled, or spent.

Calling `pexpire(key, ttlMs)` immediately after the `hmset` write lets an idle bucket self-delete from Redis once nobody is using it, bounding total memory to roughly the number of currently-active clients.

The TTL must be set to at least the time it takes the bucket to fully refill (for example twice `capacity / refillPerSec` in milliseconds), otherwise a client that is still genuinely active but pauses briefly between requests could have its key expire mid-use.

When an expired client returns, `checkRate` finds no existing key, so it treats the request as if the client were brand new and issues a full bucket — which is exactly the same behavior a first-time client gets, so correctness is preserved rather than broken by the fix.

Confirming the fix works means seeding the limiter with a large number of distinct synthetic client ids, letting the TTL window pass, and asserting that Redis key count or `used_memory` plateaus at a stable ceiling instead of continuing to climb linearly with the number of ids used.
The contract is enqueue(payload, { idempotencyKey, attempts, backoff, priority?, delay? }).
idempotencyKey is deterministically derived from the logical event, such as a hash of the event or webhook id, so the queue drops a second enqueue carrying the same key on its own.

The remaining options carry what belongs to any durable queue: retry attempts and a backoff strategy are always needed, while priority and delay are optional for when ordering or scheduling matters, worded neutrally instead of copying one library's exact field names.
The point most people miss is retention: dedup only holds if the idempotency id is kept around past the moment the job completes.

This retention can be achieved either by widening the retention window for completed-job history, or by splitting off a separate processed-key store with a TTL looked up independently of the job's own lifecycle.
Deleting completed-job history right away to save memory means the next duplicate enqueue has nothing left to compare against, so the guarantee evaporates the instant the job finishes.
The producer's job is just to write a durable record and return immediately, with no waiting and no hand-rolled retry logic of its own.
Dedup lives in the id rather than in the caller's carefulness — running exactly once is a property of the id attached to the job, not of the caller.
The interface is a single method `checkRate(clientKey) -> { allowed, remaining, retryAfterMs }` that both decides (allow/block) and records (decrements a token) in the same round-trip.
State must never live in each instance's own memory, since in-memory counting per pod behind a load balancer multiplies the effective limit by N and drifts further the more you scale out.
State is funneled into one shared store — Redis — with one key per client shaped `rl:<clientKey>` (a HASH holding `tokens` + `ts`), so every instance reads/writes against one source of truth.

Check-then-decrement must run as a single indivisible round-trip — the entire read-refill-compare-decrement-write packed into one Lua script executed via EVALSHA, since Redis runs Lua single-threaded and atomically.
Splitting the operation into separate GET then SET commands breaks correctness under concurrency: two requests arriving at once can both read the same stale value and both pass, exceeding the limit.
Two tunables are exposed: capacity (how large a burst is allowed) and refill (the long-run average rate in tokens/second) — two independent axes tuned separately.
Every key needs a TTL (e.g. PEXPIRE, ~2 × capacity/refill seconds) so a one-time client's bucket doesn't leak Redis memory forever.
Time computations must use one single clock source — `now` taken from Redis itself (TIME) rather than each instance's local clock — so skew between instances can't corrupt the lazy-refill math.
Three consumers attached to one shared queue form a work-queue, not a broadcast: RabbitMQ round-robins unacked messages across whichever consumers are on that queue.
As a result, inventory, notification and analytics would each receive only roughly a third of order.created events — never all of them.
The correct topology is to publish order.created to a fanout exchange and bind a separate, dedicated queue per service (inventory.q, notification.q, analytics.q).
The fanout exchange copies the message into each bound queue independently, so a crash or slow consumer on one queue never affects delivery to the others.
Broadcast versus load-sharing is purely a topology decision — whether consumers share one queue or each own one — not an application-code change.
Fanout ignores the routing key entirely, which is fine here since all three services want every order.created event.
If later some services only want a subset of events, a topic exchange with per-queue binding patterns is the next step up.
The semantically correct status code is 429 Too Many Requests — the request is entirely valid, there are just too many of them in a short window.
The 429 must be paired with retryAfterMs, computed from the token deficit divided by the refill rate, so the client knows precisely how long to wait rather than guessing.
Returning 403 would be wrong because it implies the client lacks permission — a permanent condition, the opposite of rate limiting's temporary 'wait, then allowed again' nature.
Returning 500 would be wrong because it makes the client/proxy read this as a server-side fault, triggering aggressive or non-standard retries, or making them stop calling entirely.

Without a precise retryAfterMs figure, every currently-limited client tends to retry in near-unison once each guesses the window has reopened, producing a fresh thundering herd on the system that just rate-limited them.
Retrying immediately, multiplied across N workers, piles more load onto an already-overloaded/down downstream, driving a death spiral.
Exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s) spreads the retries out over time so the downstream gets room to recover.
After a real outage, every job that failed together will retry back in phase at exactly the same delays, producing a new thundering herd that is merely delayed.
Jitter (e.g. randomizing the wait by roughly ±20%) de-synchronizes the jobs so they don't slam the downstream again all at once.

The worker never writes its own retry loop — it just throws on failure; the queue mechanism itself increments attemptsMade, waits the backoff delay with jitter, and re-enqueues the job, since the retry policy belongs to the queue, not the handler.
Once attemptsMade hits the configured max, the job is pushed to a DLQ instead of retrying indefinitely.
